Tsuris means troubles, worries, suffering, and aggravation — all rolled into one word. Think of it as pointing to that heavy, draining mix of problems and distress that life sometimes piles onto a person. If you have tsuris, you are burdened by difficulties that wear you down emotionally.
What makes it special — the flavor of the word

Tsuris is not just a synonym for "problems." It carries a particular emotional weight that ordinary words like "trouble" or "worry" don't fully capture. Here is what sets it apart:

  • It implies ongoing, cumulative suffering. Tsuris is rarely about a single, sudden crisis. It is more about the kind of grinding, persistent troubles that accumulate over time and exhaust you — the nagging, relentless kind of difficulty that you endure rather than quickly resolve.
  • It has a world-weary, exasperated quality. When someone says "tsuris," there is a sense of sighing resignation behind it — like, "this is just how life is, and it is a lot." It is the language of someone who has been through it, and knows it well.
  • It blends the emotional and the practical. Tsuris is not purely external (like a broken car) and not purely internal (like anxiety). It sits in the middle — it describes real problems and the emotional suffering those problems cause, as a single unified thing.
How it differs from similar words

WordWhat it misses compared to tsuris
  • "Trouble" is close, but it sounds more neutral and matter-of-fact. Tsuris sounds heavier and more emotionally loaded.
  • "Worry" is purely a mental/emotional state. Tsuris also includes the real, external problems causing the worry.
  • "Grief" typically implies loss. Tsuris does not require any specific loss — it is more general suffering and aggravation.
  • "Aggravation" is milder and often suggests irritation. Tsuris can be far more serious and painful.
  • "Hardship" focuses on difficult circumstances. Tsuris focuses more on the felt experience of those circumstances — the human suffering side of it.

Tsuris occupies its own lane: it is the word for the weight of accumulated life-troubles as felt by a person.

Tsuris is used as an uncountable (mass) noun in English. This means:

  • You do not say "a tsuris" or "two tsurises."
  • You say things like: "so much tsuris," "all this tsuris," "a lot of tsuris," "enough tsuris."
  • It functions like words such as "stress," "grief," or "suffering" — you treat it as a whole, not as individual countable units.

The word comes from Yiddish and is widely used in American English, especially in Jewish-American communities and in cities like New York where Yiddish vocabulary has deeply influenced everyday speech. However, the word has spread well beyond those communities and appears in general American conversation, literature, journalism, and comedy. It is used by people who may have no direct connection to Yiddish at all.

It fits comfortably in both casual and serious contexts. You might hear it used humorously (in a self-deprecating, "oh, the tsuris of my life!" kind of way) or with genuine sorrow when describing real suffering.
Concrete examples to lock it in

• "Being a parent gives you so much tsuris — the worry never stops."

(Parenting brings endless troubles and emotional burden.)

  • "He doesn't need your tsuris right now; he has enough of his own."

(He doesn't need your problems added to what he's already suffering through.)

  • "After everything she went through last year — the illness, the job loss, the divorce — she has had more tsuris than anyone deserves."

(She has endured an overwhelming amount of suffering and hardship.)

  • "Don't bring me tsuris on a Monday morning."

(Don't start my week by dumping your problems and drama on me.)

  • "I have enough tsuris with my landlord already."

(I already have plenty of ongoing aggravation and grief with my landlord — I don't need more.)

Tsuris means the deep, wearing, often ongoing burden of troubles, worries, and suffering — both the problems themselves and the emotional pain they cause — with a tone of weary, lived-in resignation baked right into the word.
